title: Android Inc. and Google's 2005 Acquisition
explainer: Android began as Android Inc., a small startup co-founded by Andy Rubin, before Google quietly acquired it in 2005 with no public product to show — a bet that smartphones would eventually need an open operating system. The platform wasn't originally conceived as an iPhone competitor at all; early prototypes targeted cameras and BlackBerry-style devices before pivoting to touchscreens. For anyone specializing deeply in Android, that pre-acquisition history helps explain some of the platform's early design priorities around openness and device fragmentation.

title: iPhone OS: Shrinking Mac OS X Onto a Phone (2007)
explainer: When the original iPhone shipped in 2007, Apple had two internal teams competing on the software: one adapting a lightweight Linux-based system, the other, led by Scott Forstall, compressing Mac OS X itself down to run on a phone — and the Mac OS X approach won. That ancestry is why iOS's windowing, security, and application-framework decisions still echo desktop macOS choices today, even though almost nothing about the touchscreen interface resembled a desktop. Specializing deeply in iOS effectively means specializing in the descendant of a desktop OS that was never originally designed for a touch-only device.
